utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTIN
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning to you all. Appearances for the Defence. Of course, it couldn't be but you, Mr. Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't tell me your name, Mr. Bojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUJIC
utterances.text: My name is Aleksandar Vujic, and I'm here together with John Ackerman and David Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you all. So the same question, I see that the team behind you increases. That's all my staff, Mr. Ackerman. If you have any objection, I will have them placed -- sit somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the afternoon crew that was in this Court after us broke the podium. We have scotch-taped it back together hoping it will hold. But any moment it might just fall in a heap. Claudius has gone off to find another one for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope this is not a bad omen. Mr. Cunningham, are there any preliminaries before we proceed? I don't think so. Mr. Cunningham, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Last night at dinner, Mr. Ackerman repeatedly admonished me to slow down, so I'm going to try to do that. And I would like to apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were somewhere between 16 and 33 yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The interpreters still think I'm at 78. I'll do my best, and I apologise to them. Mr. Ackerman also reminded me that this Court is quite capable of reading, so what I'm going to do is limit my remarks on implementation. I had talked yesterday that I was going to pick up with the Sanska Unska group. In reality, Mr. Ackerman is going to cover some of that. But I would like to make a few comments on the notion of implementation in Petrovac because that is an area that Ms. Korner discussed, and that is an area that the Witness, Mr. Radojko, testified. When Ms. Korner gave her closing speech, she talked about Mr. Radojko, who had talked about what would happen if the municipality didn't follow a crisis staff decision. And in summary, in his testimony at page 20139 through 40, he, in effect, said that there were two methods, two mechanisms to bring pressure on the crisis staff. One was the populous, the general population; the one -- the other one was the army. Ms. Korner suggested that the municipality certainly wouldn't call the ARK, but they would contact Pale. And when she made that argument, I don't think there is anything in the record that would support that. With respect to the Prosecution's claim made in their brief that if a -- that the presidents of the municipalities felt like they had to implement decisions or they would be replaced, I'd ask the Court to consider this fact: With a nonimplementation rate of 88 per cent, and that's viewed in the light most favourable to the Prosecution, if 88 per cent of these decisions were not being implemented and these presidents were subject to being sacked, one would think there would be a line of deposed presidents all along the road from Banja Luka down to Pale. And the fact is that never happened. I'm going to turn my talk now to the question of the alleged control of the military and the alleged control of the police. With respect to the military, the Prosecution has conceded, their witness conceded, Mr. Brown, that there was not per se subordination. And that's done in paragraph 1.108 of his report, which is Exhibit P2417. The Prosecution argument then devolves to the question, the claim that the crisis staff could cooperate -- cooperated and coordinated with the military. The notion of cooperation with the military structures by a civilian structure is nothing new, and I would cite the Court to two passages. One appearing at page 21535, an exchange between Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Brown. I would also urge the Court to look at a passage from Mr. Zoran Jokic at page 23938 through 9. And finally, note that Colonel Selak said at several locations, including page 12907 and 13273 through 74, that this sort of cooperation was logical, expected, and very, very typical. I want to turn now to the allegation of coordination. And one of the arguments made in writing during trial is there was a great deal of coordination between the military and the crisis staff, and one manifestation of that was the presence of Colonel Vujnovic as a representative to the crisis staff. Osman Selak, in his testimony at page 13270, dealt directly with this as to whether or not this was usual or unusual. And I'm going to quote his entire passage, again at page 13270. "It was a perfectly normal channel of communication between military and civilian authorities. It was only normal and logical that he" - referring to General Talic - "attended these meetings. He, in person, or any of his assistants, Vukelic, Bogojevic, or the late Gojko Vujnovic who was his assistant for organisation of civil authority in the area of responsibility of the Court." The Prosecutor next contends that there was coordination between the crisis staff and civilian structures with respect to mobilisation and disarmament. Briefly, as we've noted in our brief, the genesis or the origination of the mobilisation order as well as the disarmament order come from structures other than the ARK. P157 was from the Ministry of Defence. That's the general mobilisation. The disarmament, Exhibit P167, came from the regional secretariat for National Defence. The Prosecutor has argued that as part of this disarmament coordination, that there were no efforts ever made, and I take that back. That there were no serious efforts to disarm the Serb paramilitaries. I'm going to ask the Court to review an exchange with Milenko Savic. Milenko Savic, as the Court recalls, was the former police chief in Prnjavor who, to be fair to the Prosecution, left that post in March, April 1992. But he described meetings that he had with Stojan Zupljanin. And at these pages, I've discussed with the Court or given the Court, he discusses that. But there is one passage I would like to read very, very briefly. And this is Mr. Savic's response to the question. "Which paramilitary groups, what ethnicity was the primary focus of these meetings, if you can tell us?" Answer: "We mostly discussed Serb paramilitaries, but we also discussed other paramilitaries composed of other ethnic groups, but which were not within the scope of our municipality. We mostly discussed those that were in our territory, and we discussed what to do with them. That was my biggest problem, my most pronounced problem at the time." With regard to this claim of not doing anything or not doing enough with respect to Serb paramilitaries, again, I'd ask the Court to look at two conclusions: 15 May 1992 conclusion of the crisis staff, which said as follows: "Especially strict measures shall be implemented against any person misusing the uniform and insignia of the TO or the army without authorisation, stopping or checking people's identity or vehicles, searching dwellings or other premises." And there's a conclusion, 18 May 1992, which talks - I'm going to paraphrase - all formations that are not of the VRS or the Banja Luka security service centre must be disarmed. All those not in the armed forces or the police must return their weapons. A final area with respect to the military I'd like to address deals with logistical --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Reference to the exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Those are both out of 227, Your Honour. I don't have the -- Exhibit P227. I do not have the specific decision numbers, and I can get that for the Court at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The final area I would like to talk about because it was referenced in the Prosecutor's opening statements back in January 2002, they reference the fact that the strategic goals could not have been achieved without the logistical support of the political arm. With respect to this logistical support provided by civilian structures to the Yugoslav People's Army or its successor, this was natural. And this was confirmed by Osman Selak. And I'd like the Court to look at his response which is at page 12907, and it was also confirmed by Mr. Dejanovic from Bosanski Novi who said at page 23246 that the civilian authorities had the obligation to provide logistics support to the military in any situation in which the military was activated. And I gave the Court the wrong page number for Mr. Selak. Can I take that back and give you 13264 to 65. Turning to the question of the police who claim that the police fell under the control of the crisis staff, they argue in part, based on Section 46 of the law of internal affairs, Mr. Ackerman is going to discuss that. With respect to Exhibit P202, I would again point the Court to the testimony of BW-1 as well as Milenko Savic, both of whom testified that P202 worked absolutely no change in the chain of command that had been long established within BiH. And I'd also like to remind the Court that with respect to every witness who had the stature as or position as BT-95, none of those witnesses ever testified that P202 changed the long-standing practice that a civilian structure couldn't order the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the specific references from BW-1 and Milenko Savic's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I can give it to you at the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The final area that I want to discuss briefly with respect to the police is a claim that is made at paragraph 149 of the Prosecution's brief where the Prosecution argued that Mr. Radojko, again, of Petrovac, gave perhaps the clearest explanation of the reality of the situation; namely, whatever the legal position may or may not have been, the police did carry out certain instructions from the assembly and the crisis staff. What I'd ask the Court to do is to look at the entirety of that testimony, and this is page 20053 through 55. Because to summarise, Mr. Radojko was talking about a unique situation in Petrovac where, after that municipality left the Bihac region and joined the Banja Luka region, there was no regional control from the CSB. So in that situation, he said: "In a certain period" - and this is at page 20054 - "in a certain Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. period, there was a transitional period where the functions were being transferred from one region to another. Our police remained without any real, any kind of real control from a regional centre, and it was effectively without a functional administration." And it's in those situations, in that situation, where the police acted on orders from the municipality. Final area that I want to discuss, Your Honours, is the defendant's actions after the termination of the ARK Crisis Staff because the Prosecution alleges that he was still part of the JCE and contributed to his actions. Briefly, I'd like to remind the Court that in July of 1992, his efforts with respect to the Muslim population in Celinac, I'd like to remind the Court again of what his secretary, Drenkja Beric testified as to what his routine was in the two months that she worked for him. That's July through September of 1992. And to summarise her testimony, she testified that during that time period, he attempted to assist people of all three nations, treated all three nations -- people from all three nations the same and did his best to help Muslims in acquiring housing. Mr. Ackerman's going to talk about some of his actions at the Ministry of Housing but I'd like to remind the Court that while there, through the testimony of Boro Mandic, he insisted that the rule of law be applied. And as cited in our brief, he issued documents which attacked, in effect, police officers and VRS officers who were attempting to acquire apartments, either through force or by way of squatting. In the final exhibit with respect to the claim that Mr. Brdjanin is still marching in lockstep with the SDS leadership is Exhibit P2484. This is from the Assembly of the 23rd of November 1992. And I'd like to have the Court look at that exhibit, and I briefly want to summarise some things that are important in this. Mr. Brdjanin begins his speech by saying the following: "Krajisnik has asked to have at least a minimum of respect for dignity, and I agree to that." Mr. Brdjanin continues: "I had a very unpleasant conversation with Mr. Karadzic, and I did not even think of answering him." And during the course of this speech he makes, Mr. Brdjanin suggests that the Serb Democratic Party is the long arm of the communist party. He criticises the party; criticises war profiteers. And I think it's especially instructive for the Court when you look at this exhibit, P2484, is to see how Mr. Krajisnik reacts as the speaker of the assembly. He gives Mr. Brdjanin a chance to back off his statements that are critical of the party, and Mr. Brdjanin does not. That's important because I think it still shows one of the themes that we've seen throughout Mr. Brdjanin's relationship with Pale within -- with the upper echelons of the SDS, as that is -- in many, many occasions, on many, many different issues, he was totally at odds with them. That concludes my remarks. I thank the Chamber for the opportunity to address you, and I'll turn the lectern over to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- come a long way together. Sometimes that journey we have done has been an easy one and most often it has been a hard one. There have been bumps in this road that we have travelled, and there were times when I wondered, and I suppose you wondered, if we would ever make it to this day. But we did. We did make it. And I think we've made it here very well. I think we were careful along the way to try to make sure that this was a fair trial. During this journey, Your Honours, I was mostly struck in a role as observer, I suppose, by how Your Honours invariably followed the evidence so closely and paid such close attention, and how you were so much involved in the evidence in this case. And I say that from having experience in a case where one of the Judges slept through a great deal of the case. And I appreciate that none of you did that. We don't have to raise that issue on appeal. When you questioned witnesses, you asked good questions. And I don't -- I think the Prosecutor would join me. I don't think we could have asked for a more attentive Trial Chamber. And for that, I know all of us are grateful. I want to begin by making it clear, Your Honours, that the argument that I will make to you today is solely for your benefit. I'm not speaking to Banja Luka; I'm not speaking to Belgrade; I'm not speaking to anyone but you. As far as I'm concerned, they could turn off the television that goes out from here because I have no interest in my remarks going beyond this Trial Chamber. You're the people who I want to hear what I have to say today. I want to begin just very briefly talking a bit about the challenge to the indictment that was raised in our brief. The Prosecution responded to that challenge basically saying that it wouldn't be fair for us to make that challenge now because we didn't raise the issue earlier. And if we thought the indictment was not sufficient, we should have made that clear at an earlier date. It's not the burden of the Defence, Your Honour, to perfect the indictment. That's the burden of the Prosecution. The Prosecution is correct that we do have a burden to raise the issue. We did that. We raised the issue. We got a favourable ruling that clearly instructed the Prosecutor as to its obligations. Once we raise the issue and get that favourable ruling, I believe we have no obligation to go beyond that. It then becomes the burden of the Prosecution to follow those orders and to abide by that ruling. To understand exactly what I'm talking about, we have to start with the decision of this Trial Chamber on the objections raised by Radoslav Brdjanin to the form of the indictment. The Prosecution was ordered to file a further amended indictment which, (a), complies with the pleading principles discussed in Sections 4 and 5 of the Talic decision; and (b), pleads as material facts the precise role of the accused and the nature of the accused's individual criminal responsibility. That's in paragraph 18 of that order. According to the Oxford English Reference Dictionary, material means "important, essential, or relevant." In other words, the Prosecution must plead the important, essential, and relevant facts of its case. The order of Trial Chamber II is not ambiguous. To understand what that order means when it talks about -- when it refers the Prosecutor to Sections 4 and 5 of the Talic decision of 20 February 2001, we can look at that. With regard to superior responsibility, the Chamber said: "In a case based upon superior responsibility, what is most material is the relationship between the accused and the others who did the acts for which he is alleged to be responsible, and the conduct of the accused by which he may be found to have known or had reason to know that the acts were about to be done or had been done by those others, and to have failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts or to punish the persons who did them." That's paragraph 19. With regard to individual responsibility, the Chamber said: "In a case based upon individual responsibility where it is not alleged that the accused personally did the acts for which he is to be held responsible, where the accused is being placed in greater proximity to the acts of other persons for which he is alleged to be responsible, then he is, for superior responsibility." Again, what is most material is the conduct of the accused by which he may be found to have planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of those acts. But more precision is required in relation to the material facts relating to those acts of other persons than is required for an allegation of superior responsibility. The Prosecution -- the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber decision then came down following these orders where the Kupreskic Appeals Chamber basically followed the position that had been taken in this case by Trial Chamber II. That case stood for the following: "It is, of course, possible that an indictment may not plead the material facts with the requisite degree of specificity because the necessary information is not in the Prosecution's possession. However, in such a situation, doubt must arise as to whether it is fair to the accused for the trial to proceed. In this connection, the Appeals Chamber emphasises that the Prosecution's expected to know its case before it goes to trial. It is not acceptable for the Prosecution to omit the material aspects of its main allegations in the indictment with the aim of moulding the case against the accused in the course of the trial depending on how the evidence unfolds." Now, Your Honours, that's exactly what the Prosecution has done in this case. In addition to the matters that we cited in the main brief, consider the matter of Mr. Brdjanin's speeches and statements. The Prosecution can't claim regarding those statements and speeches that they were not in their possession at the time of the indictment. That cannot be an excuse for failing to plead the speeches and statements as material facts, but they did fail to plead it. If you look in the indictment, you'll not find one word that the speeches and statements of Mr. Brdjanin were a material fact that they were alleging against him. Not one. And yet, their entire closing brief in this case relies very heavily on them. I will admit that they spoke of them in their opening statement, and I'll admit that they spoke of them in their Pre-Trial Brief. But that's two and a half years, Your Honour, after the indictment -- the initial indictment in this case. Two and a half years passed with numerous amendments to this indictment, and never did the Prosecution allege as a material fact that they were relying on Mr. Brdjanin's speeches, two and a half years in which investigation could have been carried out regarding those allegations and was not. Is this fair? Is this justice? I think not. I now want to talk about some of the things that the Prosecution told you in their final argument. One of the things that has been an issue in this case almost throughout is that meeting of the assembly on May 12th of 1992 where Dragan Kalinic addressed the assembly, and then several speakers later Mr. Brdjanin responds. The Prosecutor wants you to believe and accept that what Mr. Brdjanin was responding to and saying that he agreed with was Mr. Kalinic's words as follows: "Among all the issues this assembly should decide on, the most important one is this: Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation? I say this with a reason, and I must instantly add, knowing who other enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically and militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies liquidating and eliminating their key people," and he goes on to say "he doesn't hesitate to choose the first option." Now, if Mr. Brdjanin is agreeing with that statement, then he is agreeing that the option is not negotiation but war. That's clear. But what is it that Mr. Brdjanin says at the very end of his remarks? He says: "That is why in the negotiations, that is why in the negotiations we can ask for this corridor in exchange for some parts that are not important for us. And should it come to the worst, the corridor even if only buswide, will have to be established by military means." And he says "that will be all. Thank you." So he doesn't accept that war is the option; he accepts that negotiation is. And he says in the negotiations Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. here's what we should do. So it's some other part of that Kalinic speech, and there are many parts to it that he must be agreeing with. The Prosecutor discussed the issue of credibility of witnesses. We've really not talked about that in our briefs, and I don't intend to spend very much time on it in my argument today. As I said at the beginning, we've observed that Your Honours have paid very careful attention to the witnesses, to their demeanour, to the way they answered their questions, to the consistency or inconsistency of their testimonies and statements. And all those things you observed, and I'm sure noted at the time, I believe very little would be served by retracing that ground except to the limited extent that I have done so in our brief and may do so on occasion in these remarks. Crisis staff minutes. The Prosecutor has talked at length about crisis staff minutes. First of all, I would suggest that it would be totally inappropriate for Your Honours to draw any conclusions from the fact that they're missing, from the fact that the Prosecution has failed to produce them. You should not draw any conclusion from that at all. It's a non-issue in this case. Mr. Cunningham read you that part from the Sanska Unska document which indicates that maybe minutes weren't really being kept. At least, maybe up until that time. But I can tell you this: You heard us on more than one occasion ask witnesses if they knew where those minutes were, if they could please try to find them. We would really love to have them. And if they exist, we would like to have them here, Your Honour. And the same is true for the minutes of the crisis staff in Celinac, because we suggest to you those minutes would -- well, I will not suggest what they would show. I can only say about that that the Prosecution has not proved that Mr. Brdjanin attended even one meeting of that Celinac Crisis Staff. The Prosecutor spoke at length to you about missing documents and suggested you could draw certain inferences from the fact that documents were missing from various municipalities. I suggest with regard to all the missing documents that no inference can be drawn from the failure of the Prosecution to produce them in aid of their case. The only way you could do that is if you could infer that the documents really did exist, that they really were available, and the Prosecution did not bring them. Then I think the law is that you can then infer that they would have been helpful to the Defence if the Prosecution didn't bring them and they were available. But there's no evidence that they were available, so that would not even be a permissible inference. The Prosecution suggested that one thing you could infer from the fact that these documents were missing was that they would have been able to prove a great, higher level of implementation had they been able to get their hands on these documents. That's also an inference you cannot make. It's pure speculation. As Mr. Cunningham pointed out to you yesterday, the nonimplementation rate by Mr. Treanor's calculations, if you calculate them properly, is 96.4 per cent. The variant A/B document, this is it. It's P25. The Prosecutor spoke about this at length. First of all, the Prosecutor said to you it was issued by the main board of the SDS. I don't know that there's any evidence of that. If you look at the document itself, the issuing authority according to the document on the last page, page 8, is the SDS Crisis Staff, an organisation otherwise unknown to the record in this case. It's noteworthy, I think, we think, that this document is not directed to any regional organisations, but directly to municipalities. We believe it's clear that the provisions of this document, in fact, were implemented in many of the municipalities. It's also clear that this had no connection and nothing to do with the ARK Crisis Staff. There may have been, Your Honour, joint criminal enterprises going on, but we think they may have been multiple, a separate enterprise going on in each municipality. And certainly in no case was the accused part of any of those joint criminal enterprises. There was no such enterprise functioning at the level of ARK. Throughout her remarks, the Prosecutor kept talking to you and suggesting to you that matters were not raised in the final brief of the accused. This has absolutely no legal significance at all. The plea of the accused in this case is not guilty. This places the burden solely upon the Prosecution to prove each and every one of its allegations beyond a reasonable doubt. It's not a relief from that burden that the Defence fails to contest some matter in its final brief. Everything not admitted by the Defence is contested by the Defence, and that's the law. Exhibit P251, Ms. Korner tells you that this document shows that Brdjanin was thinking just like Karadzic regarding annihilation of the Muslims. I suggest to you it's anything but that. He's suggesting that they work together with the Muslims to solve the economic problems of the region by removing the blockade of the corridor to Serbia. All you have to do is look at the document. Now, of course one problem with this document is we have no idea where it came from. It's just a piece of newsprint. We don't know what publication it's from. But setting that aside, Brdjanin talks about power shortages which have brought the overall economy to the verge of collapse. He talks about households that have electricity for only two or three hours a day. It talks about how the citizens of Banja Luka may move relatively safely and without fear of provocations in a radius of about 40 kilometres in all four directions. Brdjanin deems it indispensable to secure a corridor through the northern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina to Serbia which would be equally a way to the world for the Serbs and the Muslims from the Cazin and Bihac Krajinas. If we do not manage to resolve the issue of annexing Krajina to Serbia peacefully, we shall literally have to resort to war, says Brdjanin. In that case, the Muslim and Croat people will have to pay the price, because they are precisely on the charted route of the future road. He's talking about the corridor. He's talking about it having been blocked by Croatian and Muslim forces preventing access to Serbia. It goes on to say that Brdjanin think that is the most efficient solution is agreement between the warring parties on lifting the blockade on the road via Tuzla and Bijeljina for, according to him, wars have been waged so far for corridors. And if no agreement is reached, a corridor will be breached toward Belgrade sooner or later. In that context, he believes that Fikret Abdic, a Muslim, could be a major asset in the negotiations as he could bring influence to bear on extremists from the Cazin Krajina and negotiate with the central authorities in Sarajevo. This is nothing like the Karadzic speeches about annihilation. I want to talk briefly about assembly speeches. Ms. Korner was quoting the assembly speeches of numerous persons in her remarks on Monday. They were from Exhibit P20, the 15 October 1991 assembly meeting. One of the things this Chamber must bear in mind, which Ms. Korner overlooks, is that in an assembly such as the one she is talking about, or in any legislature in the world, people rise and speak and make proposals. What they say is not policy. What people say in those sessions is their ideas of what policy should be, what they would like it to be. But what they say is not policy. And when Ms. Korner refers you to these statements, she is suggesting to you that this is policy of the SDS. This is policy of the assembly. And until it is shown that a proposal by a member has been adopted and put into effect by that assembly, it's not policy at all. It's just a speech. And that's all it is. And it has no other significance. Because someone makes a speech does not make it policy. And I will discuss some of Mr. Brdjanin's speeches that were ignored by the assembly, not adopted by the assembly. The Prosecution -- well, Mr. Cunningham has already discussed this, so I don't think I'll spend time doing that. In Monday's remarks, Ms. Korner is talking about I believe it's the Djeric document. And she says this. This is on -- the time signature is 12:55:31 on Monday. "Your Honour, that is why we say, even though the April instructions themselves specifically don't say "regional crisis staff," it is absolutely clear on the evidence that the SDS intended and did establish a regional crisis staff." It's not absolutely clear on the evidence. In fact, there's no evidence at all that the SDS established a regional crisis staff. It's absolutely not clear on the evidence. In fact, the thing that I think is significant is that the Autonomous Region of Krajina was not the only autonomous region. But it's the only one in which there's any evidence that there was ever a crisis staff. And if there was some SDS policy to set up crisis staffs in all the regions, I think we would have heard about crisis staffs in other regions, but we did not. Mr. Brdjanin's signatures on documents. The Prosecution wants you to believe that it makes no difference whether Mr. Brdjanin signed documents or not. If his name appears on them, it's good enough, as far as the Prosecution is concerned. And we respectfully disagree with that. We believe that one of two things must happen before a document and its contents can be attributed to Mr. Brdjanin. The Prosecution must either prove beyond a reasonable doubt that his signature appears on the document, or prove beyond a reasonable doubt that he specifically authorised another person to sign it on his behalf. With the exception of about three documents, the Prosecution has proved neither of those things. You'll remember at the beginning of the case, the Prosecutor was distressed that we were denying that the signatures on the documents were Mr. Brdjanin's. And then additionally distressed when we refused to supply handwriting exemplars, and when this Court upheld that refusal. So when it became apparent that they were not going to be able to prove that Mr. Brdjanin signed those documents, they then began to treat it as unimportant. But I suggest to you that it is singularly important. The Prosecutor wants you to accept their assertion that there was a plan to kill the Muslims and Croats of the Krajina. They fail, however, to explain to you why it was that when thousands of Croats and Muslims from the Krajina were put into various detention facilities by people who had lots of guns and lots of bullets, these people were not all killed. If the plan was to kill the Muslims and Croats, that was the opportunity to do it. But the vast majority of those people were released from those camps, exchanged from those camps. There are notable and horrible exceptions where people were killed. But the vast majority were not. Exhibit P185 are conclusions from the ARK Crisis Staff meeting of 11 May 1992. And this deals with a couple of issues. The first of those: "The deadline for surrender of the illegally acquired weapons is hereby extended to 2400 hours on 14 May 1992." The Prosecution suggests to you that the whole issue of disarmament was a pretext for attacking the villages in the various municipalities, and that the whole idea of disarmament was it was only directed to Muslims and Croats. Now, why, if what you're doing is setting up a pretext, do you extend the deadline? It makes no sense. It makes no sense that you would do that. The other thing that -- I'll come to it later. Article 46 of the Law on Internal Affairs. This is a giant red herring, Your Honour. I had thought that the Prosecution had abandoned this, but it came up again in argument. Article 46 does not say what the Prosecution has been suggesting it says. Poor Mr. Sadikovic. He was led into agreeing with them about it. I mean, he wanted to help them any way Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he could. And I don't blame him. The Serbs had treated him badly. And he wouldn't mind getting a bit of revenge if he could. So he was led into a position where he agreed that in emergencies things were different, and Article 46 gave extraordinary powers to civil authorities over the police. It does exactly the opposite. Exactly the opposite. Any lawyer reading it will understand that. Listen. "In the discharge of duties and responsibilities to protect the constitutional order, the lives and personal safety of people, to protect property from destruction, damage, and theft, to maintain law and order and the safety of road traffic, as well as in the event of general danger caused by natural disasters, epidemics, and so forth, the minister" - that's the minister of the interior, MUP - "the minister or his authorised representative or, in emergencies, other authorised officers" - meaning persons authorised by the minister - "may issue special orders to citizens, enterprises, and other legal entities." In other words, what that's saying is that in these kinds of emergencies, the minister of the interior may designate persons, probably police, but may designate persons to issue orders in special circumstances. In other words, the police could order the crisis staff to do things under this. Not the other way around. Absolutely not. All of these calls for disarmament, if you read them, each one of them, every time says "enforce the law." "Enforce the law." Gather up illegally held weapons. Gather up illegally held ammunition. They're asking that the law be enforced. The Prosecution suggests otherwise, but must prove it beyond a reasonable doubt. The police officer out there enforcing the law, the police officer out there in his car, the police officer out there on his beat receives an order to gather up illegally held weapons and ammunition. Where is the evidence in this case of anyone suggesting to the police officers who were supposed to carry out these orders that they really don't mean what they say? Now, Mr. Police officer, please understand that this order saying all illegally held weapons, but we really don't mean that. There's no evidence of that, of those officers being so instructed. None at all. What they get is an order to gather up illegally held weapons. And I suggest that's what they tried to do. On Tuesday, Ms. Korner showed you some charts. P2650 showed the distribution of killings. P2648 showed the distribution of exhumations. P2649 showed the distribution of camps. P2647 showed the distribution of religious property destruction. I urge you to look at those again because they are striking. One of the striking features is the virtual forest that you will see in the municipalities west of Banja Luka. Every one of them. It looks like a forest of markers in those municipalities that we have called the renegade municipalities. But what is more striking, I suggest, and very telling in terms of this case is the virtual absence of markings in Banja Luka and Celinac, especially Celinac. If there's one municipality in the Krajina where Mr. Brdjanin had influence, it was Celinac. But if you look, there are virtually no killings. The Sugic brothers the exception. No exhumations. No camps. Two religious structures. Now, if Brdjanin was the leader of some genocidal campaign as the Prosecution tries to convince you, wouldn't you expect him to try to set an example in the municipality where he at least had some significant influence? On the contrary. It appears that he was able to prevent as long as he was there, until he went off to the ARK Crisis Staff. He was able to prevent extreme activities in Celinac, and to a lesser extent in Banja Luka. Where he had no significant influence, things were terrible, west of Banja Luka, up there in Kotor Varos. Prosecution Exhibit P2356, this is the Drljaca document establishing Omarska and talking about the secrecy with which that should be treated. The Prosecution says, well, no, it really wasn't all that secret because look at the distribution list. And I want you to look at the distribution list, because the distribution list is really, really important. It went to the Prijedor Crisis Staff. It went to the security services coordinators, Mijic, Jesic, and Lieutenant Colonel Majstorovic. It went to the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka, his immediate superior. He was probably required to send it to them. It went to the police chief, which is him. It went to the security chief who works for him. It went to the general manager of the iron ore mines which is where they were setting up the camp, so they probably needed to know about it. And a copy went to the files. Where was there not a copy sent? To the Autonomous Region of Krajina. To the ARK Crisis Staff. No copy went there. The most powerful civilian organ in the ARK, according to the Prosecution, was not sent a copy of this. That's significant. And I think -- I've not had time to go through and look at everything, but I think if you look at the distribution lists of other documents in this case, nothing went to the ARK Crisis Staff. Nothing. P2356, this was talked about yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the same document, isn't it? Because the previous one, what you described, the Drljaca document on Omarska, is -- you told us was P2356.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it's not. That's the wrong number. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I'm pointing this out. You know, I mean, it's a good thing that Ms. Korner did not stand up and accuse you of trying to mislead the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: P1267. I deserve that remark, too. Thank you. P2356 was referred to by Ms. Korner yesterday. And it's a document we don't know the date of issued by -- says it was issued by Miro Mladjenovic, I think. It says "Mradjenovic," but I think it's probably Mladjenovic from the association of Bosanska Krajina Municipalities. And it talks about some statements made by Mr. Brdjanin. And she said this is significant in showing that Mr. Brdjanin agreed with Mr. Karadzic about various matters. If you look at the document, Your Honour, it has nothing to do with the Krajina. This is early. This is when the war is going on in Croatia. And Mr. Brdjanin begins his remarks with this: "Due to the new situation in Okucani, that's Croatia, and Stara Gradiska, that's Croatia, where the army had to retreat under order to its positions and the Serbian people in Okucani have remained in Ustasha encirclement we demand..." And he's demanding a mobilisation, a preparation to defend the border, and assistance to the Serbian people that are surrounded up there. And he says we have no right to leave the Serbian people in Croatia to the mercy of the Ustasha warriors for our grandfathers would curse us and our grandchildren would be ashamed of us. That refers directly back to what had happened during World War II where the Serbian people were left to the mercy of the Ustasha, and we can't let that happen again. Nothing to do with ARK, nothing to do with the Krajina. Only with regard to what was happening across the border in Croatia. Yesterday, Ms. Korner talked about the role that Mr. Brdjanin played in Celinac. The evidence shows that when he became president of the ARK Crisis Staff, he effectively left Celinac and had virtually nothing to do with events there after that. The minutes of the - and I'm sorry, I don't have the exact cite for you - but the minutes of the Celinac Assembly at one point talk about someone taking his place because he doesn't come to meetings any more. The records do indicate that he was made a member of the crisis staff, but as I mentioned there's no indication at all that he ever attended a meeting. Ms. Korner referred to Exhibit P1981 for the proposition that by the end of April, 770 Muslims had left Celinac. And I suggest that that simply cannot be true. It cannot be true that 770 Muslims had left Celinac by the end of April because there were 1.860 Muslims still there in April -- in August, which was basically the entire Muslim community in Celinac. She spoke of a speech that Brdjanin made at the end of August in 1992 saying that this tells you about his intent. He says in that speech: "Those who are not loyal are free to go" - speaking of Muslim and Croats. Free to go. Not "must leave." Not "will be expelled." But "free to go." If you believe the Muslim witnesses from Banja Luka, virtually everyone had already left by the end of August in any event. I think Krzic says that most of the Muslims left by May, which I suggest is simply not the case. I think the Muslims left Banja Luka in 1995, and there's evidence of that. I want to finally talk about that 1993 speech that we saw the tape of again yesterday, which the Prosecution concedes is 1993 and couldn't have any effect upon any of the offences alleged in this case. I think that speech is not nearly as clear as to what Mr. Brdjanin means as the Prosecution would like you to believe. If you listen to it carefully, before he makes the remark about non-Christian scum, he talks about the leftists and what the leftists are trying to do. Now, the leftists are communists. That's who the leftists are. And it may very well be when he speaks about non-Christian scum, he's speaking about the communists and what the leftists, the communists, are trying to do. Never does he say anything about Muslims by name. And certainly communists could, in many places, be described as non-Christian because in many places they not only prohibited religion, they destroyed religious buildings. I want to say just one thing about implementation and Mr. Brdjanin's speeches. These tend to be the kind of two big issues that are before you. We get into little traps occasionally where we get so focussed on implementation that we begin to believe that that's the issue. We begin to believe if there was implementation, then the Prosecution has proved the case; and if there was not, they haven't. But I suggest to you that's not the case. If you look at all of the conclusions and decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff, you don't see any conclusions or decisions demanding the commission of an offence. You don't see any decisions or conclusions demanding ethnic cleansing. You don't see any decisions or conclusions suggesting killings, beatings, murders, tortures, or any of those things. If every one of the ARK Crisis Staff conclusions and decisions had been implemented in every one of the municipalities and nothing more, no crimes would have been committed. None. None. The other thing we get into, if the Prosecution can prove that Mr. Brdjanin made some of the speeches and statements that he is alleged to have made, then he must be guilty. If they can't prove it, then he's not. That's another rabbit trail. They have to go way beyond that he made speeches. They have to prove to you that those were heard. They have to prove to you that those had an effect. They have to prove to you that people did things because of those speeches. Look at that forest on those charts west of Banja Luka. They have not proved that anybody out there ever heard Mr. Brdjanin ever say anything. That's where the bad things happened. So those two myths need to be exploded. And that's what I have to say about the Prosecutor's arguments to you. I now want to tell you the 50 things that the Prosecution wants you to ignore. 50 things they want you to pay no attention to. And for good reason. The first thing the Prosecution wants you to pay no attention to, Your Honours, is Exhibit DB271. It's a significant part of the Prosecution's case that people were dismissed because of their ethnicity. Civil and military. DB271, 16 July 1992, document issued by Colonel General Ratko Mladic addressed to among other places, the 1st Krajina Corps, says this: "All officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who are judged by the commands of corps and independent units to have proved themselves in combat action and who want to sign the oath and give a written statement that they accept citizenship of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina may remain in active military service in the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Not ethnicity, loyalty. There's not an army in the world that would keep someone who is disloyal, who is on the other side of the conflict, who is working as a spy in your midst. But the issue is not what your nationality is; it's what your loyalty is. Now, they want you to ignore that because if you don't, it can raise a reasonable doubt, and you might have to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. So you say, well, this was sent to the 1st Krajina Corps, but it didn't have any impact there. DB272, three days later, 19 July, a document signed by General Talic marked "urgent" repeats the language. "All officers of Muslim and Croatian nationality who in the opinion of the brigade commands, independent units and corps command, for headquarters support units have proved themselves in combat action who want to sign the solemn declaration and a written statement that they will take on the nationality of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina may remain in active military service." And we know that some did. I think you'll recall Naum Golic telling you that when he was serving, he was serving under a Croat officer. His commander was a Croat. They want you to ignore DB284. They want you to ignore DB284 because it shows that the paramilitaries that they were trying to disarm were Serb paramilitaries. It's a 1st Krajina Corps document dated 30 July 1992, refers to disarmament of paramilitary units. It says this: "Paramilitary formations are present in the areas of responsibility of all corps, and they are mostly behind the lines of combat operations in the rear and in populated areas. They rarely enter areas of combat operations, and then most often behind SRBH army units as they liberate territory and settlements with looting as their principal motive." The order after that preamble, it goes on, it says this: "Offer all paramilitary formations and their leaders, if they do honestly intend to serve the rightful struggle for survival of the Serbian people, an opportunity to join the regular SRBH army units and assign them in accordance with their military occupational specialties and military skills." These are clearly Serb paramilitary units. "Do not include in units individuals and groups which have been involved in crimes and looting or have committed other criminal acts. Disarm and arrest them and bring criminal charges against them in SRBH army courts regardless of their citizenship. In cooperation with SRBH MUP, disarm and arrest paramilitary formations, groups, and individuals belonging to them who refuse to come under the unified command of the SRBH Army and bring criminal charges against them corresponding to the criminal acts they committed. I forbid the existence of any paramilitary units, groups, and individuals in the territory of the SRBH. By 15 August 1992 at the latest, disarm all paramilitary formations and submit a detailed report on this." They want you to ignore that because that could raise a reasonable doubt and might cause you to have to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. P1261. P1261 is a conclusion from the Prijedor Crisis Staff signed by its chairman, Dr. Milan Kovacevic. "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality does not accept and considers invalid all decisions by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopted before 22 June 1992." Now, Your Honours, that's all of them with the exception of about two or three. That's the whole body. This shows the municipalities were operating independently. It shows the effect of Article 35 of the ARK statute that municipalities knew that they didn't have to follow ARK Crisis Staff decisions. And most important, it shows that absolutely nothing happened to people who ignored the ARK Crisis Staff, contrary to the Prosecutor's contention that people would be dismissed, which is a bizarre contention. These were people who were elected to their positions by the people. That anyone had the power to dismiss someone who was elected by the people is a stretch for which there's absolutely no support. The Prosecutor deals with this by causing it -- calling it an odd document. Any document that disagrees with their theory of the case, I guess, is an odd document. They want you to ignore this because it raises a reasonable doubt and might cause you to have to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. On 30 January 2002, way back in ancient history when we started this case, Mr. Cayley is examining Dr. Robert Donia. Mr. Cayley says: "Now, you state" - and this is page 1111 [Realtime transcript read in error "111"] of the transcript - "now you state in your report that on the 15th of April 1992, TO units in Muslim-led municipalities were placed under a unified command and became the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then there's a break, and then he asks: "Just referring briefly to the region of the Krajina, from your knowledge, if you can answer this question, how effective was the Bosnian Army in that area?" Donia says: "I don't really think there was a Bosnian Army per se in the Krajina. It was really these local TO units which were poorly armed, and its effectiveness was very low." Mr. Cayley: "But you do state that the Bosnian Army had the advantage in terms of manpower. Is that correct?" Answer: "It appears that at this time, yes, they did. The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because that could raise a reasonable doubt and cause you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. Let's look at Dr. Donia again. This time, page 1245, this time during cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman. Question: "One of the -- one of the announced justifications for the formation of ZOBK and then ARK was that there was a contention by persons in the Krajina area that the concentration of economic resources in Sarajevo was causing the area to be economically neglected." Dr. Donia says: "Yes." The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because that could raise a reasonable doubt and cause you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. Number 7: Dr. Donia again. Page 1246, question by Mr. Ackerman: "It is not your contention, is it, that this whole concept of regionalisation was something that was invented by and emanated from the main board of the SDS?" Answer: "No, it's not." No. Prosecution wants you to ignore that because that could raise a reasonable doubt in your minds and cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. I'll continue, Your Honour, with number 8 after the break.

We'll have a break resuming at -- Mr. Ackerman, do you have any problems with concluding today, you think?
