utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thanks to the usher, I now have the mother of all podiums, and I'll be able to beat on it without fear of breaking it when I get down to the end of my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can always blame it on others. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Korner reminded me during the break that I had misquoted the exhibit regarding Muslim leaving Celinac. She says that the exhibit says that "by April, there were only 770 Muslims left in Celinac." By April of 1993, well, then, let's just forget the whole thing. All right. There will be more to say about that, then, as we get down through this list. Let's go to number 8 of the 50 things that the Prosecution wants you to ignore. This is the testimony of Boro Blagojevic at page 21709 on 29 October 2003, examined by Mr. Cunningham. Question: "I understand that you're not currently affiliated with a political party, but were you ever affiliated with the SDS?" "No. I have never been a member of the SDS." So one of the perhaps two employees of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was not even a member of the SDS. The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it might raise a reasonable doubt and cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. Mr. Predrag Radic, page 21977, 3 November 2003, examined by Mr. Ackerman. "The crisis staff in relation to the army, did Mr. Brdjanin or the crisis staff itself exercise any control of any kind over the army?" Answer: "Nobody but the presidency or the first figure of the presidency could exert any influence over the army or the police. Nobody had that power. I would like to remind this Honourable Chamber that not before the war, not during the war, not even today civilian organs have had any influence on the army. Not even today when there is a mayor of Banja Luka, that person cannot issue any orders to the police. All he can do is issue a request which is then forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior, and then it's the Ministry of the Interior which issues an implementation order. This question has already been put to me, whether Brdjanin was in the position to issue orders to the police or to the army, and I answered then and I'm answering now that no, he was never in that position. He was never in the position to issue any order to any military unit." Question: "And your answer also includes the police? I think you've included both the police and the military in your answer, that neither Brdjanin nor the ARK Crisis Staff had any control or position to order. Am I correct?" Answer: "I was already asked that, and I answered that he was not in the position to do that. He didn't have any competence of that kind. Nobody would have obeyed any such order coming from him." The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it raises a reasonable doubt and might cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. Again, testimony, Predrag Radic, page 22009, 3 November, questioned by Mr. Ackerman: "Well, did Mr. Brdjanin have authority over the people in Prijedor? Could he order those people to do things and not do things? Did he have that kind of authority?" Answer: "No, he didn't." The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because that could raise a reasonable doubt and cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. Again, testimony of Predrag Radic, page 22340, examined by Mr. Ackerman, 7 November 2003: "When was it that most of the non-Serb population that actually decided to leave, when was it that the vast bulk of them left? What year?" And after a little preliminary, Mr. Radic said: "The bulk of the people left in May 1995 during the Operation Flash and Storm." The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it raises a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. reasonable doubt and might cause you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. Exhibit P95, this is an extract from the minutes of the 10th session of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka, 14 December 1991. The document reveals that on that day, the assembly received a report of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre on the criminal and other illegal activities of Veljko Milankovic and other members of a paramilitary formation from Prnjavor. JNA representatives read a report from the Banja Luka Corps command on the arrest of Milankovic and other persons. In the conclusions reached that day, number 2, "the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina neither recognises nor supports the establishment of paramilitary formations, nor will it participate in their funding. It condemns every activity related to carrying out duties that lie within the competence of legal organs and security services. The Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina recognises the JNA and units under its command as the sole armed force and requests that they act forcefully to protect the people and territories that recognise them as their armed force." Interesting limitation there. Number 3: "After a lengthy debate on the activity of the paramilitary formation from Prnjavor, under the command of Veljko Milankovic, the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina fully accepted and supported the measures and activities of the security organs of the JNA 5th Corps and the Banja Luka Security Services Centre." Now, the Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it raises a reasonable doubt and might cause you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. Prosecution tells you in the indictment, in its arguments that Mr. Brdjanin was the person designated as chief propagandist, as the person to take control of the press, the television, the radio. In that connection, you should take a look at P107. P107 is an article from Glas of 11 February 1992. I'm not going to read it to you. It is very long. Suffice it to say that it is a document, an article, from that newspaper that is highly critical of Mr. Brdjanin, not the kind of article you would find in a newspaper under his control. In that connection, you should also look at P110, where the Celinac National Defence Council responds and points out how outrageously wrong that article critical of Brdjanin actually was. Now, the Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it's an article of faith with the Prosecution that Mr. Brdjanin was controlling the media. This raises a reasonable doubt about that and might cause you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. Exhibit P80, this is the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Now, Ms. Korner conceded that the municipal presidents, because of the way the system had operated for so many years, were people who were reluctant to give up authority. And of course they are. Any time anybody achieves a position of authority, they're reluctant to give up any of it. And that reluctance is set out in stark language in Article 35 of the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. This is an association that was created by the presidents of the various municipalities, voluntarily. And one thing they made certain of when they created the statute of that association was that they were not ceding any authority to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That's why you see in that statute this language: "Decisions and conclusions of the Assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of municipalities." And not otherwise. They maintained their power. They maintained their authority. They didn't give it to this organisation. And you see clearly that that's the case, that they were asserting Article 35 as a basis for ignoring the ARK Crisis Staff because the ARK Crisis Staff tried, and I suggest failed miserably, to solve that problem by purporting to amend Article 35. Now, obviously, the Prosecution wants you to ignore that because that basically destroys their whole theory of this case. It certainly raises a reasonable doubt and would require you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. Their witness, Mr. Treanor, page 20916. Mr. Treanor, who was one of the best witnesses for the Defence in this case. At 20916, questioned by Mr. Ackerman: "I want to look now at Article 35" - referring to the one we just talked about from the ARK Statute - "and I think if nothing else this highlights the completely voluntary nature of this association. If you look at the second paragraph of Article 35, decisions and conclusions of the assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of municipalities." Mr. Treanor: "Yes." Question: "In other words, the decisions and conclusions of the ARK Assembly were only binding on municipalities once their assemblies accepted them?" Treanor: "Yes, that's correct." Mr. Treanor again, page 20949, 15 October 2003, questioned by Mr. Ackerman, referring to Article 38 of the ARK Statute, which is the article, Your Honours, which deals with amendment to the statute. Question: "Article 38 talks about the manner in which the statute may be amended, and it says that a proposal to engage in the procedure of amending the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina may be submitted by the assembly, the assemblies of the associated municipalities, and the executive council. The proposal referred to in the preceding paragraph shall be communicated to the assemblies of the associated municipalities for their consideration and for the purpose of obtaining their opinions. And then after their opinions have been obtained, or after a given deadline has expired, the assembly shall consider the draft enactment on amendments or additions to the statute and transmit it to the assemblies of the associated municipalities to obtain their approval. And finally, having attained the approval of the associated municipalities, the assembly may then declare the amendments and additions to the statute adopted." Answer: Yes, that's correct." "So that's the procedure that would have to be carried out to amend, for instance, Article 35 of the statute. Correct?" Answer: "Yes." And at the bottom of page 20950, "I'm suggesting to you that the crisis staff had no authority to amend the statute of ARK unless they complied with Article 38." Answer: "Yes, yes. That would certainly be true." Now, Your Honour, they really want you to ignore that because that disagrees with their theories. It raises a reasonable doubt. It might require you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. While the Prosecution, this is the 17th thing they want you to ignore. While the Prosecution tells you how important Mr. Brdjanin was in the SDS, what a huge role he played in the SDS, how he was one of the main SDS actors, they want you to ignore the fact that he was never even a member of the SDS main board. Exhibit P157 has been talked about over and over at length. The Prosecution wants you to ignore parts of this documents or to treat them as not really meaning what they say. That's paragraph 4, which says: "The command of the TO and police forces is under the exclusive authority of the professional staff, and therefore any interference regarding the command of the TO or the use of the police forces must be prevented." That should be ignored. They want you to ignore paragraph 8, that the crisis staff has the obligation to provide working and living conditions for the JNA members to ensure a fair attitude toward the JNA officers and soldiers and to prevent them from being humiliated or insulted in any way. Now, the Prosecution would say to you, Gee, this shows close cooperation between military and civilian authorities; in fact, control. Until you look at paragraph 9, which uses the same language, to say that the crisis staff shall provide working conditions for the international peace and relief organisations and ensure the unimpeded transport of relief convoys to their destinations. Surely, the Prosecution would not argue that that shows control by the crisis staff over relief organisations. They want you to ignore that this document was not directed to any regional crisis staff. Although they suggest to you that in paragraph 14 when it says: "Submit weekly reports to the regional and state organisations of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina" that that must refer to the regional association of the ARK. And that's not a necessary conclusion at all. The legitimate regional organisations that existed way before the war started were the regional police organisation, the CSB, and the regional military organisation, the 5th Krajina Corps, which became the 1st Krajina Corps, the Banja Luka Corps. P626, this is a document from the Sanski Most Crisis Staff dated 28 April 1992. This is about a week before there was ever any ARK Crisis Staff. This is about a week -- more than a week before the Sajic disarmament order of the 4th of May. The Sanski Most Crisis Staff says this: "All citizens in the area of Sanski Most Municipality who possess any kind of weapon shall hand it in to the public security station, the closest unit of the Yugoslav People's Army, or the staff of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Municipality of Sanski Most. Citizens who have private weapons with a license from a competent organ and members of armed Territorial Defence formations, active service and reserve police and the Yugoslav People's Army are exempt from this decision." This shows that disarmament was being ordered in Sanski Most before Colonel Sajic issued his order, before anything came from the crisis staff about that. That substantially detracts from the Prosecution's theory that disarmament was a major goal of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the ARK Crisis Staff, and that it was a juggernaut set in motion by them. They want you to ignore this because it detracts from that theory, establishes a reasonable doubt, and might cause you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin. P165. P165 is an article from Glas. This was during a time apparently when Glas couldn't even get enough paper to publish on a daily basis because this is an issue dated 30 April, 1 and 2 May. It's a press conference with Mr. Brdjanin dealing with personnel changes in enterprises. Mr. Brdjanin reportedly says: "Only people loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina can hold managing positions in Banja Luka and the Bosnian Krajina." Loyalty, not ethnicity. Loyalty. "I am especially pleased that among the reports and requests of workers for the replacements of individual managers there are managers of all the nationalities." He's pleased with that. "Which means that people want honourable people to head their organisations." The Prosecution wants you to ignore this because it raises a reasonable doubt as to their theories and might cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. Your Honours will recall that the SDS took over power in Prijedor at the end of April, before the creation of the ARK Crisis Staff. The Prosecution would like you to ignore that. Exhibit P1181 and similar documents, there are a number, and Your Honours saw them all. I think I presented them to the witness -- I can't remember his name now. He was a witness from Prijedor. Documents showing that people were being dismissed from their positions in Prijedor substantially before the creation of the ARK Crisis Staff. It's P1181 and documents in that same number range. You could look at one of my favourite documents, DB118. This is the order by Gojko Klickovic to the command of the 1st Krajina Brigade where he orders them to destroy three bridges in Krupa. And then says they don't really have to if they think it's not wise from a military point of view. But this is dated 24 April 1992, before there was any ARK Crisis Staff. Ethnic cleansing, according to the Prosecutor, was an enterprise of the ARK Crisis Staff that Mr. Brdjanin was the leader of. You should Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. look at P2077. This is another document from Krupa dated 5 April 1992, a whole month before there was any ARK Crisis Staff, apparently signed by "Crisis Staff commander," Gojko Klickovic, in which he says this: "It is hereby ordered to carry out a partial evacuation of the population from the following neighbourhoods and streets" and then he lists a bunch of neighbourhoods and streets. So here is Klickovic ordering ethnic cleansing in Krupa a month before there was ever any ARK Crisis Staff. Of course, the Prosecution wants you to ignore that document because it could raise a reasonable doubt and cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. A couple of interesting documents that speak of the power of the ARK Crisis Staff, P183, P532. On 9 May 1992, the ARK Crisis Staff reaches the following conclusion: Due to abuses in its work, the Atlas Travel Agency is prohibited from further work. Now, you know from the testimony of Mr. Fazlagic, he kept on working. He got special dispensation from the municipality. Totally ignored this document. On 3 June, almost a month later, crisis staff tries again: "At its session held on 3 June 1992, the Autonomous Region of Krajina issued a decision to terminate the operation of the Atlas Primaturs Travel Agency." And again, according to Mr. Fazlagic, that one failed. The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it raises a reasonable doubt regarding the power of the ARK Crisis Staff and might cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. At page 28 of our brief, we quote from transcript page 23072 some testimony from Dobrivoje Vidic. He's talking about the ARK and decisions and how they were adopted and so forth. He says: "I know how this was done. It wasn't done in a serious manner. I know how decisions were adopted. Anyone wrote whatever they wished. Mr. Boro Blagojevic would sometimes add things. You'd never know at the next session what he had added. It was a comedy. Mr. Blagojevic, he drafted these documents later. We had quite a few disagreements over that, and I always strenuously protested. And that is why the validity of these documents was always in question, because none of the documents were ever adopted at the next session." Now, if you look at P185, you see a curious example of what he's talking about. P185 is a conclusion, set of conclusions, of the ARK Crisis Staff dated 11 May 1992. The heading: "Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, conclusion number 3, we hereby express our support for the work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Now, that's crazy. They're saying "we hereby express our support for our work." It shows you what Mr. Vidic means when he said it was a comedy. It was. "We hereby express our support for the work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" said by the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff. That's comedy, folks. The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it could raise a reasonable doubt and cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. P192, conclusion of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff, 13 May 1992. Conclusion number 1, third paragraph: "Persons that are absolutely loyal to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina have to occupy managing positions in the companies." Loyalty. Not ethnicity. Prosecution wants you to ignore that. Raises a reasonable doubt. Might cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. I think, Your Honours, that there's probably more than 50, and I'm going to talk about more than 50 because reason number 28 is really two. You should look at Exhibit P194 to start with. This is part of the comedy that Mr. Vidic talked about. On 14 May 1992, the crisis staff made the following conclusion: "The presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall immediately define the borders of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Now, they are purporting here to instruct the Presidency of SRBiH to do something, which they clearly would not have the competence to do. I think this will help you in deciphering the meaning of these conclusions from the ARK Crisis Staff. From this, you can tell that when they say somebody "shall" immediately do something, what they really mean is "should," "that would be a good idea," "it would be nice if." But it's not a directive. If you look at P227, you see a similar comedy. Paragraph 7: "The government the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is to immediately prescribe punishment for violations of the curfew." Again, they are purporting to instruct the government of SRBiH, which they clearly have no competence to do. But it could help you in deciphering meaning when they say someone is "to do" something; what they mean, "it would be a good idea if," "it would be nice if." And that's what they mean in paragraph 14 of that document where they say "for the time being, the 5th Corps is to" - same language -- "take over the Kosmos Air Force Maintenance and Production Complex until the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina comes to a final decision." What they're saying is "that would be a good idea," "it would be nice." The Prosecution wants you to ignore the comedic aspects of this crisis staff because it raises a reasonable doubt and could cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. P227, 26 May 1992, this is one in a long of those crisis staff documents where the crisis staff keeps saying "Hey, you out there, we are the highest organ of authority, pay attention to us." And nobody pays attention. So a week later they say "hey, you out there, we are the highest organ of authority. Look at us. Pay attention to us." And nobody does. They don't have to keep saying that if it's true. They just don't. This is an organisation that is suffering from being ignored, and they are crying about it. Look at paragraph 1 of P227. "The work of the crisis staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina has absolute support since it is now the highest organ of authority in the Autonomous Region of Krajina as the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina cannot function due to objective and subjective circumstances." 26 May. That's important. 26 May. Look at P209, 27 May. P209, 27 May: "Pursuant" -- the next day. "Pursuant to Article 17 of the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina at its session held on 27 May 1992 adopted the following..." And then they adopt the appointment of a negotiating team. So on the 26th, the crisis staff says "we're the highest organ of authority because the assembly can't meet" and the next day the assembly meets. And they say, when the assembly meets that day, it's pursuant to Article 17 of the statute. If you look at Article 17 of P80, it says: "The Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina is the main organ of authority of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And then if you look finally at P48, this one's dated 6 June 1992: "On behalf of the Serbian people of the Krajina, the presidency of the Autonomous Region of Krajina hereby renounces the legitimacy of Nenad Kecmanovic and Mirko Pejanovic to represent the Serbian people in any capacity," a document from the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina signed by its president, Vojo Kupresanin. The Prosecution, of course, wants you to ignore all of those because they fly in the face of their theory, they establish a reasonable doubt, and might cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. We're up to number 30, Your Honours. P1726, I suggest to you that this document shows why Vujnovic was attending ARK Crisis Staff sessions. To report on the economic situation in municipalities, and it confirms the testimony that it was a place where municipal authorities gathered to complain. On 17 June 1992 in P1726, Vujnovic submits a report. He says this: "At a meeting of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina held on 17 June 1992, it was decided that elected deputies should begin forming civilian governments in the Municipalities of Donji Vakuf and Derventa with the help of the units of the 1st Krajina Corps in that area. The economy has totally collapsed in the area of the Autonomous Region of Bosnian Krajina because of the impossibility of obtaining production materials or exporting finished products and a total financial blockade. Throughout the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, there is a general shortage of electrical power, petrol, money, and some foodstuffs." The Prosecution talks about people being dismissed from their jobs. They fail to distinguish, though, Your Honour, between those who were dismissed for loyalty reasons and those who lost their jobs because of the huge downturn in the economy. Muslims, Serbs, Croats, all were thrown out of work when trade between the Krajina and Croatia, and Serbia and Sarajevo was brought to a halt. Testimony of Boro Mandic, page 21252, 21 October 2003, talking about the composition of the executive board in Celinac while Mr. Brdjanin was in charge, uncontested by the Prosecution. Question: "How was it being a nonmember of the SDS that you were able to secure this position of secretary with the executive board?" Answer: "Let me tell you how this happened. The executive board at its very beginning was composed mostly of members of the Serbian Democratic Party, although I must say before this Trial Chamber that Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin did not agree with that. He insisted on the executive board to consist of experts in their respective fields, regardless of their party affiliation, regardless of their religious affiliation or ethnical background. And very soon after that, probably against a lot of opposition in his party, he managed to succeed in changing the composition of the executive board so that from then on members of the executive board were also people who were not members of the SDS. Other members who participated in the very important work of the executive board were people who were never members of the SDS before that or after that. For example, Nenad Josip was the secretary for economy, and the vice-president for the executive board, and he was appointed on the insistence of Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. Mr. Vlado Vrhovac was the director of the revenue administration. Then Nemanja Miljanovic who was also a lawyer and who was born in a mixed marriage, he was a misdemeanor judge in that term of office. His position was very important." So in Celinac, in the executive board, where Mr. Brdjanin had authority, he employed people for their skills, not their ethnicity, not their party association, exactly what the Prosecution suggests to you he was against. They want you to ignore this because it raises a reasonable doubt. I want to go into private session for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 31 July 2003, Your Honours heard from Milorad Dodik. I refer you to page 20516 of his testimony. Cross-examining by

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "I'm talking to you about Brdjanin's role in the crisis staff. You said on page 5, line 23 of the English version, `in other words, if Brdjanin wanted to implement anything with the crisis staff, he had to ask for the approval of Radic. Without that, he couldn't have done anything.' Do you stand by that statement today?" Answer: "Well, that was my opinion. I was not present at these meetings. But this is an opinion that corroborates the previously mentioned position; namely, that Mr. Brdjanin was not the most influential member of that staff. And quite simply, that people were there who had far greater power and who were in such offices. I already mentioned the chief of the police, the presidents of the municipalities, the president of the SDS, so they had these positions. They held these offices. They were on the staff ex officio, and the implementation of these decisions depended on them." Question: "Now, just so we can save a little bit of time, when you say to us that it is your impression or you have the opinion, that's based not only upon your observations at the time but on your conversations with people since that time, up until fairly recent times. Am I correct in that? In other words, you're not just guessing. This is based upon something that you observed and have heard." Answer: "Yes, that's correct." Your Honour, we have to go back into private session again now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 22567 of the testimony -- just in passing, Your Honours, I never thought I'd stand in front of a Court and refer to page 22567 of a record. This record is monumental. It's incredible. This is Rajko Kalabic, 12 November 2003. Questioned by

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Now, we all know that some bad things happened in Kljuc. Could Mr. Brdjanin or the ARK Crisis Staff have prevented those things from happening?" Answer: "Mr. Brdjanin could not have prevented anything that happened in Kljuc itself because after the 27th of May 1992, and those events, of course, he could not influence those. And later developments occurred spontaneously and were often beyond the control of those who made efforts to keep them under control. So his influence there was nonexistent." Same witness, Your Honour, page 24828 -- I'm sorry, this is not the same witness. We have to go back into closed session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go back now to the witness Boro Mandic. We're at page 21279 of the transcript, where the witness says this, in answer to a rather long question by Judge Agius: "Well, I can say with absolute certainty" -- I'm going to have to read the question because the answer makes no sense without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Sir, I'm going to read from the transcript that I have right here in front of me, and then you've heard what Mr. Ackerman said, and you tell me whether you want -- what you want to have on record. `In most cases, municipalities did not allow this to take place because they probably wanted to give the abandoned flats to the refugees who arrived from Croatia, from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember very well, and there are a number of decisions.'

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SAYS
utterances.text: "This is where Mr. Ackerman said to you that there are hundreds of decisions." And then quote: "There are hundreds of decisions in our ministry testifying to that when we started working on the 15th of March 1993 and dealing with those appeals, Mr. Brdjanin..." et cetera. Judge: "Did you see there were such decisions or hundreds of such decisions"? "What I can say with absolute certainty that there are hundreds, certainly more than one hundred, and probably hundreds. Not decisions, determinations. The ministry makes determinations." Then Mr. Ackerman: "In the process of making those determinations, did Mr. Brdjanin make any distinction between members of different ethnic groups? Did he treat members of different ethnic groups differently?" Answer: "No. On the contrary, every decision that had to do with the swap of apartments or the rationalisation of housing space had two opposing parties involved. One of the parties was always a non-Serb. Mr. Brdjanin insisted that we go by the book; that is, by the law, and the law required us to approve the exchange of apartments or rationalisation of housing space, and we did that. It was always signed by Mr. Brdjanin or one of his deputies, and all of these determinations were confirmed by the Supreme Court." And Your Honours will recall that we then introduced records supporting what he said, DB154 through DB159, and DB166 through DB169, which are all written determinations in favour of Muslims and Croats. So it's not just his word, but the documentary evidence that supports it. The Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it speaks of Mr. Brdjanin's feelings regarding the law and regarding non-Serb persons, raises a reasonable doubt, and might cause you to acquit him. DB189. DB189 is a document dated 22 February 2002. As it's a document that was requested by us from the Ministry of Defence, we wanted to know and we wanted the Court to know about Mr. Brdjanin's working Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. obligation during this time. And it is significant, and I'll show you why. According to the records of the Ministry of Defence, from 6 April 1992 until 30 June 1992, Mr. Brdjanin's working obligation was in the Municipality of Celinac on the position of president of the executive board. From 1 July 1992 to 14 December 1992, it was in the Government of Republika Srpska as vice-president of RS and minister for urbanism, housing, and public utility activities and ecology. What is clearly missing from that is the ARK Crisis Staff. And it's missing, I suggest to you, because it was never recognised as a legitimate organ and could not have been a way to satisfy a working obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next document I want you to look at, Your Honours, one of the 50 that the Prosecution wants you to ignore, is DB379A. This document comes from the Banja Luka public security station. And it talks about registration and deregistration in Banja Luka for the period 1 January 1992 to 31 October 1992. Now, you'll recall that there was significant testimony by Bosniak witnesses early in the case about if you were going to leave Banja Luka you had to go through this huge process of deregistration and getting authority from the police and all those kinds of things. Through that period of time, the records of the Banja Luka public security station, from January through October of 1992, in other words, encompassing the entire period of the ARK Crisis Staff, of persons coming to Banja Luka and registering there, 3.440 Serbs, 1.607 Croats, and 1.647 Muslims came to Banja Luka and registered in Banja Luka during that period of time. Persons who deregistered to leave Banja Luka: 1.242 Serbs; 2.278 Croats; 3.011 Muslims. This totally contradicts the testimony of many of the Bosniak witnesses that people were leaving Banja Luka in droves in early 1992. And it totally supports the testimony of Mr. Radic that the vast majority left in 1995, certainly after October of 1992 and the period of the crisis staff. And of course, the Prosecution wants you to ignore that because it raises a reasonable doubt, might cause you to find Mr. Brdjanin not guilty. Mr. Cunningham talked about this yesterday. I want to just briefly mention it to you again, because I think it is so important. It speaks of the credibility of witnesses and it speaks of this issue about Muslims leaving Banja Luka. It's the testimony of Muharem Krzic, page 1788. Question by Mr. Ackerman: "Now, Mr. Krzic, you see what we are looking at here. It's an Article from Newsday written by Roy Gutman September 25 1992. You know Mr. Gutman, do you not?" "Yes." "Did you have meetings with Mr. Gutman"? "Yes." "You've actually had Mr. Gutman as a guest in your home, have you not?" "Not a guest, as a visitor." "As a visitor in your home, you've gotten to respect him, and you believe he is a respectable journalist. Correct?" "Yes." "Could we look then at page 2 of this document, and look down toward the bottom, the yellow part, down toward the bottom, starting with 'until now.' 'Until now, Banja Luka the principal city in northern Bosnia has been largely spared the terror tactics of ethnic cleansing, the process of emptying territory of unwanted ethnic groups.'" That's what Mr. Gutman wrote in September of 1992. Do you agree with him?" Answer: "I don't agree."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at 5 to 1.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next document that I would refer you to is DB344. DB344 is that article from the publication Patriot of 12 August 2003 written by Boro Sendic. Your Honours will recall -- no, this wasn't -- this was an open document, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. Don't expect me to know that. But someone will be checking it, whether it was under seal or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Better check before we go any further, I suppose. It was not, all right. Your Honour will recall that this is the document where Sendic claims the following -- claims that Brdjanin demanded the arrest of he and Grahovac and Mladjenovic for setting up a paramilitary group, the Wolves of Vucak. What he says is this exactly, talking about the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina: "The assembly was convened on 15 November by its president Vojo Kupresanin. The first speaker was the assembly vice-president Radoslav Brdjanin, and he immediately attacked Grahovac. What did he think he was doing setting up some paramilitary unit without consulting the assembly, spending money on it, buying uniforms and so forth, with Sendic and Mladjenovic?" And near the bottom, "Grahovac behaved in a slightly distant manner, as though he was disgusted by the whole thing. He briefly wanted to help the Slavonian people because they had asked him to. He was pleased that Mladjenovic and Sendic had formed a unit of volunteers who proved their worth in these few clashes. The assembly did not decide on anything. Brdjanin's proposal that the three of us be charged for harmful and inappropriate behaviour was not accepted." Now, that's interesting in itself, but what confirms in many ways what is said in this article is that reunion at Mount Kozara of the people who were responsible and involved in the taking down of the transmitter tower there. And who was at that reunion in Grahovac, Mladjenovic, Milankovic was dead or I'm sure he would have been there. The same group, the same group that Sendic talks about here. Not Mr. Brdjanin. He wasn't there. The Witness Mehmed Talic, page 24146. Bosniak from Celinac. He talks about encountering Brdjanin at the municipal building with a problem. Brdjanin says to him: Go to the office. I'll be up there in a minute. And he says: "And I came to the office, and we sat down together, and we talked about all the problems, about everything. And he asked me, Talic, what is bothering you? And I told him what it was. And he said, yes, Mr. Brdjanin will help you. "At 12.00, maybe 11.30 or 12.00, I'm not sure, the meeting was supposed to be held at the Celinac municipal office. So we went out at 11.30 from his office. At that time, Mile Maksimovic came out. I don't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know what he was, chief of the ministry or something. And he said from the door, Mr. Maksimovic, make me a special permit and secure me a driver and a car so that Meho can be taken. When you make this permit, bring it to my office. I'm bringing a stamp, and I will stamp it so that Meho can go and bring his daughter back. And he said very well. Ilija came back, and he made the certificate for the driver and the vehicle, and he took it to the office. And Rajko Orasanin was the driver of the car. He took me to Kotor Varos, and I went and I brought my daughter back. And I returned. Everything went well. I found my daughter in Kotor Varos, and I managed to bring her back. So this is what Mr. Brdjanin did for me." Now, contrary to what the Prosecutor told you, this was not a permit signed by Mr. Brdjanin. This doesn't show Mr. Brdjanin had power in Kotor Varos. It's a permit signed by what Mr. Talic believed was chief of the ministry, Mr. Maksimovic. The next page, 24145, "go ahead and tell the Chamber about the encounter between you and Brdjanin at the municipal building." Actually, that's the beginning of the part that I have already read to you. I think we don't need to go into that. It's actually the preceding page. Again, Your Honour, from Mehmed Talic, page 24152: Question: "All right. I have a lot of questions to ask you about some of the things that you said. You talked at one point of being in front of the municipal building, and Mr. Brdjanin had arrived and gone inside. And you said you could hear his voice from inside the building. Do you have any recollection as to what it was you heard him saying?" Answer: "I couldn't hear exactly what he was saying, but I could just hear him shouting, raising his voice up there to those officials. I heard that personally, that he was shouting at them. This was the second or the third floor, the windows were closed, of course. So it wasn't possible to hear everything that he was saying. But I know very well that he ordered that we should be put in the elementary school, and that there should be a guard for us. We were not detained. We could go out freely. They were really protecting us." And he talks about the 1.860 of them. I asked him then: "Who do you believe is responsible for the 1860 persons in Celinac being protected and placed in the school and being protected? Who do you think is responsible for that? Mr. Brdjanin?" Answer: "Mr. Brdjanin and three other Serbs who reported to the military police." And when he says reported to the military police, that was the report that if the buses left town, they would be ambushed. Question, and now this is a different subject, Your Honour, but goes to what the Prosecution told you yesterday about Muslims leaving Celinac. This is 24154. "You told the Chamber that in 1992, several of the young people, and the words you used were `they left to seek their fortunes elsewhere.' My question is, were these young people forced to leave, or did they leave of their own free will?" Answer: "They left of their own free will." Question: "When you left, were you forced to leave or did you leave of your own free will?" Answer: "Of my own free will. No one forced me to. No one. We were merely protected." Now, Your Honour, there were 1.860 Muslims in Celinac on that day who this witness says had their lives saved by Mr. Brdjanin. Presumably, the Prosecution had access to a large number of those 1.860 people. And if this were not the case, I suggest they would have brought you a witness in rebuttal to say it was not the case. I want you to look again at P229. This is that Sanska Unska group, the first document we know of that was issued by them. 7 June of 1992, representatives from Bihac, Bosanski Petrovac, Srpska Krupa, Sanski Most, Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, and Kljuc sent -- these conclusions they adopted were sent to the crisis staff of the Autonomous Region of Banja Luka. And they made certain demands. "It is necessary to declare a state of war in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina within the next three days." That was not done. Number two: "Within the next three days, we request a clear position from the highest authorities of the Serbian Republic of BH on the question of forging a land corridor to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." The ARK Crisis Staff would have had no competence to deal with that one, but it was not done. Number 4: "We demand that the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, and particularly General Momir Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps, purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslims and Croats. We believe that they cannot fight against their own people and that they are now involved in intelligence and other activities in the 1st Krajina Corps that are of interest to Ustasha forces and members of the so-called Alija's Territorial Defence. Deadline for completion, seven days." We know from the first documents I referred you to today that people who were loyal, whether they were Muslim or Croat, to the Serbian Republic were able to remain in the military, and some did. "We absolutely demand that within the next three days, the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina clearly define the borders of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." That was not done. Number 6: "All seven municipalities in our subregion agree that Muslims and Croats should move out of our municipalities until a level is reached where Serbian authority can be maintained and implemented on its own territory in each of these municipalities. In this respect, we request that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina provide a corridor for the resettlement of Muslims and Croats to Central Bosnia and Alija's independent state of BH because they voted for it. If the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Banja Luka fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka." Now, this is exactly the opposite of what the Prosecution is suggesting to you. This is this subregional group saying "we want the ARK to assist us in the ethnic cleansing of our municipalities." It's not the ARK ordering them to do it. It's them ordering the ARK to help them, or else they will do something drastic. And again, this corridor was not provided by the ARK Crisis Staff. It was ignored. So what are the consequences of the ARK Crisis Staff ignoring this group of municipalities? What then did they do? Well, they met again about a week later. On the 14th of June, P247. They said: "We think the work of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina under wartime circumstances should be much more serious and that it's politicians and experts should pay more attention to the problems in all constituent municipalities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina." Now, this time, Your Honours, meeting at Korcanica were representatives from Srpska Krupa, Bosanski Petrovac, Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Prijedor, Sanski Most. So after saying that the crisis staff should be more serious, they say "accordingly, we propose that Vojo Kupresanin be appointed president of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, given the position he currently occupies, president of the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and belongs to -" something that's unclear. So they are saying there, get rid of Brdjanin and put Kupresanin in his place. And a little further down, they tell you why. "Accordingly, personnel changes should be made in the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and with a view to urgently breaking with individuals who have decided to obstruct the work of the Serbian Democratic Party in the Autonomous Region of Krajina and to question the lofty goals which have galvanised the Serbian people." They are saying in no uncertain terms that Mr. Brdjanin has decided to obstruct the work of the Serbian Democratic Party and the ARK, and to question the lofty goals which have galvanised the Serbian people. They are saying that this project, this enterprise that we're trying to carry out is being thwarted by Mr. Brdjanin. He is standing in the way. He is an obstacle. You must replace him and put Kupresanin there who will carry out these tasks. Now, it's one thing for me to say that Mr. Brdjanin was not part of a joint criminal enterprise. It's one thing for me to argue that. But when his peers argue that on the 14th of June 1992, when his peers take the position that he is not participating in this process, that is a powerful, powerful, powerful thing. The Prosecution really wants you to ignore this because this establishes a reasonable doubt, beyond a reasonable doubt, and with this, with this kind of criticism at that time, from those people, he's not part of any joint criminal enterprise. Your Honour, that concludes the -- 50 of the reasons why you should acquit Mr. Brdjanin, the 50 things the Prosecution want you to ignore. A long time ago, and I don't know when, the Prosecution set out to deal with matters that had occurred in the Krajina. And they reasoned that it would make sense to look for, indict, and prosecute the person who headed the military organisation in the Krajina at the time. They found out that was the 5th and then the 1st Krajina Corps, and that it was headed by General Talic, and he was indicted. The reason that it would make sense to look for, indict the person who led the police in the Autonomous Region of Krajina during the time involved, they determined that was Stojan Zupljanin. He was indicted. Not yet arrested. And they determined that it would make sense to look for and prosecute the civilian leader of that region during that period of time. And so they looked for some regional authority and found the Autonomous Region of Krajina. They looked for who was in charge of that and decided, well, it must be the crisis staff and Mr. Brdjanin. Now, that was not a bad way to look at how to prosecute what had happened in the Krajina. That was a reasonable approach. The problem was this: There had long been a regional organisation of the military. The Banja Luka Corps had been there for years. And it became the 1st Krajina Corps later on. There had long been a regional organisation of the police, the CSB in Banja Luka. But there wasn't any regional civilian authority. It simply did not exist. The best they could find was this Autonomous Region of Krajina. And by the time it became clear that their quest regarding a civilian authority was one that held no water, it was too late. Mr. Brdjanin was indicted. He was at this Tribunal, and they had to go forward with the case. But I suggest to you it became clear to them even that they were on the wrong track. There's a book that's well known in Texas where I come from that tells a story about a man who goes out, stays out virtually all night drinking heavily. Comes home about 5.30, 6.00 in the morning and goes in the backyard and hops into the hammock where his wife finds him that morning. And she starts giving him a hard time, alleging that he was out all night and partying and carrying on. And he says, no, no, no. He said I came home about 11.30, and I didn't want to wake you and so I just came out here and got in the hammock. She said, that's a complete lie. I looked at midnight, I looked at 3.00, and you weren't there. So that's just a total lie. And he said Well, that's my story and I'm sticking to it. And that's the Prosecution's story in this case. And they are sticking to it. There's a lot of evidence in this case that's very ambiguous, to say the least. From that ambiguous, I suggest the Chamber must always Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. draw the inference most favourable to the accused, if it's a reasonable inference. When you look at the charges in the indictment and ask if they were proved, if you say maybe not, you're stating a reasonable doubt. If you look carefully at the Prosecutor's final brief, look carefully at the arguments they have made to you, you find that what they have created is a house of cards. It's just a house of cards. And the problem with that house of cards is it's full of jokers. And if you remove a joker, the house falls. And their case falls. When you look at this evidence the Prosecutor wants you to ignore, I suggest you're left with only one choice: This case has not been proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Mr. Brdjanin must be acquitted on all counts. I'm about to sit down now, which I must tell you is hard. I have carried the burden of Mr. Brdjanin's case since July of 1999. It has been my task to rise to his defence whenever I could and to try to find the words to say that would be the right words to help him. In just a moment, I will have said the last word that I'll be able to say on Mr. Brdjanin's behalf, and I ask myself, have I said everything I should have said? Have I done everything I should have done? Have I made every argument that I should have made? Have I gone too far at times and erred in that way? I hope not. I think not. I think my job is to do everything I can ethically to help my client. It's hard to sit down and know that I'll not be able to speak on his behalf again in this case. But then trust has to begin somewhere. And we place our trust in you to consider this case carefully, responsibly, to do justice, as it's your job to do. I can ask no more. I want to close with the words of Justice Robert Jackson, as he opened the trial of the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg. He said: "We must summon such detachment and intellectual integrity to our task that this trial will commend itself to posterity, as fulfilling humanity's aspirations to do justice." Thank you, Your Honours, for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, under Rule 86(A), I have the -- sorry, we have the right to present a rebuttal argument. Your Honour, I can deal with what I want to say, and it really -- it would have been otherwise raised as objections to a couple of the things that were said. So if, Your Honour, if I may deal with that now, because I know we're not sitting tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, how long is it going to take you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to restrict yourself to the 10 minutes because we need another 5 minutes or so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I gave a warning, if I can put it that way to those who I met from the following case to say that we might be -- have to run over a little bit. Your Honour, can I deal first of all with the question of the indictment that Mr. Ackerman raised again this morning. Most of our arguments, all of our arguments, have been expressed in the written response. But I do want to say this because this has been raised again as part of the speech. First of all, Your Honours, if you look at the indictment on which this case proceeded in January of 2002, this was the fourth amended indictment. There are two things which should be said. First, there was an unambiguous order, not only from Your Honour, but from Judge Hunt that if there were any objections still remaining to the amount of detail given in this indictment, and it was known in this Tribunal as the most detailed indictment ever, ever to be drafted by a Prosecution, then those objections had to be raised by Judge Hunt's order within 30 days and by Your Honour's order by the beginning of the trial. Your Honour, the Defence simply cannot under any jurisprudence whether of this Tribunal or national jurisprudence decline to comply with an order, and then say at the end of the day, this was a defective indictment. That's the first thing. Second, Your Honour, the main complaint is that it did not make it clear what the Prosecution's case against Mr. Brdjanin was. If Your Honour looks -- if Your Honours, look, please, at paragraphs 10 of the original indictment, it is stated that "the president of the ARK Crisis Staff was Radoslav Brdjanin." At the bottom of that paragraph, "amongst its other actions, the crisis staff took control of the media, continued the campaign of propaganda against the non-Serbs as a key instrument in the implementation of the aforementioned plan." At paragraph 16, "Radoslav Brdjanin was a prominent member of the SDS" and I will skip the next words. "As such, from the early stages, he played a leading role in the takeover of power by the SDS, in particular with respect to the propaganda campaign." And I should read on actually. "Which was an essential component of the SDS plan to create a Serbian state." Your Honour, that deals, as I say -- the remainder of our arguments are set out carefully in the brief. Your Honour, the second matter that I want to deal with is briefly, one of the last things that Mr. Cunningham said, and I think he must have misunderstood what I said. He said that Ms. Korner suggested that the municipality - he's dealing with Bosanski Petrovac and Mr. Radojko - certainly wouldn't call the ARK, but they would contact Pale. Your Honour, what I actually said was in relation to the removal of -- Mr. Radojko's assertion of the removal -- I've now got so many bits of paper in this -- but what I was actually saying is that the ARK Crisis Staff couldn't remove the heads of municipalities, but that Pale could, and it was clear that the people thought that the complaint would be made to Pale. That's what I said, not that they weren't going to Pale. So I think that was a misunderstanding. Your Honour, more importantly and more seriously, the question of the Celinac assertions now made by Mr. Ackerman. He has already corrected what he said that I had said; namely, that 770 people had left by April 1992. I was referring to the document that shows that 770 were left in April of 1993. But, Your Honour, he then went on to say this. Your Honour, this is -- he's referring to me. "She spoke of a speech that Brdjanin made at the end of August in 1992, saying this tells you about his intent. He says in that speech `those who are not loyal are free to go, speaking of Muslims and Croats, free to go, not must leave." Now, Your Honour, I need to go into private session for a moment because I'm going to have to quote the exact words of the witness who gave evidence in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please. What's the problem, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, not a very long time ago, Mr. Brdjanin referred to my saying that Mr. Talic had a permit signed by Mr. Brdjanin. First of all -- Mr. Ackerman. Did I say Mr. Brdjanin? I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what you said. You said Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman referred to me saying... Right. Can I -- could I have the part of my speech back from yesterday. Right. I've found that. Your Honour, what I actually said was, and this is at page 12 of yesterday's transcript: "Your Honours may remember that Mr. Brdjanin, according to Mr. Talic, was able to provide Mr. Talic not only with a car but Your Honours this is at page 24186 of the transcript, a driver, but also a special permission permit which enabled me to bring my daughter over..." At no stage did I ever allege that Mr. Brdjanin had signed the permit. But the actual evidence which was given by Mr. Talic is this: "Mr. Brdjanin called me to come to Celinac" - this is page 24145 - "I met him on the staircase, and I said, Mr. Brdjanin, I would like to speak to you. And he said yes, very well." This was in chief to Mr. Ackerman. "Go to the office. I'll be up there in a minute. And I came to the office, and we sat down together, and we talked about all the problems, about everything. And he asked me, Talic, what is bothering you? And I told him what it was. And he said, yes, Mr. Brdjanin will help you." He was obviously using the third person. "We went out at 11.30 from his office." I've missed out two lines. "At that time, Mile Maksimovic came out. I don't know what he was, chief of the ministry or something. And he said from the door" - that's he, being Mr. Brdjanin - "Mr. Maksimovic, make me a special permit and secure me a driver and car so that Meho can be taken. When you make this permit, bring it to my office. I'm bringing a stamp, and I will stamp it so that Meho can go and bring his daughter back. And he said very well." And Your Honour, I'm not going to go into the part of the -- about coming to the checkpoints because I've already reminded Your Honours. Your Honours, again, we would simply invite Your Honours as we did with Mr. Radojko to read through the whole of that evidence. And finally, Your Honour, and I must say this because we've had this mantra being repeated just in case Your Honours didn't understand the point almost at the end of each point that Mr. Ackerman was making "the Prosecution wants you to ignore" this particular document "because it raises a reasonable doubt and might cause you to acquit Mr. Brdjanin." There are two points I want to make. The first is, the majority of the documents that Mr. Ackerman referred to were entered into evidence by us on behalf of the Prosecution because we took the view that all documents that we were in possession of which were relevant to the issues should be before Your Honour. The second matter is this: At no stage have we ever suggested that Your Honours should ignore any evidence in this case. My very last words to Your Honours yesterday were this: "Your Honours, we say finally, if Your Honours consider all the evidence in this case dispassionately and objectively as we know that you will," and then we asked you to return the opposite verdict from Mr. Ackerman. Thank you, Your Honours. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Korner. Mr. Ackerman, is there a rejoinder? Thank you. But it's not over yet. And I'll try to be as concise as possible. Ms. Korner, Mr. Ackerman, when I was very young, I was taught not to look behind when the journey lies ahead. A very useful advice indeed, based on the wisdom accumulated by our ancestors, especially when the past does not auger well for the future. When I became a judge in Malta several years ago, it suddenly dawned on me that whoever coined that wise adage could not have had court proceedings in mind. How could I, as a judge in any particular case, not look behind as the journey in that case lay ahead? As a judge, I soon learned that the journey ahead at any given moment very much depended on what lay behind. In a few minutes, we shall adjourn this case for judgement. A long and laborious, certainly complex and difficult journey lies ahead. And day in, day out, Judge Janu, Judge Taya, and myself, together with our precious staff will be constantly looking behind to the proceedings in this case, looking back at all the testimony heard, at all the documents tendered, of course at the arguments and submissions, at our notes. We shall consider everything. And at the end, when we would have put all the evidence and our deliberations on the scales of justice, we shall come to a decision sometime towards the end of August. When we concluded the evidence stage, I made a short speech on behalf of the Trial Chamber thanking everyone. We are going to thank you all again. Counsel and those who work outside the courtroom behind the scenes, so to say, to assist you in your difficult work; the clerical staff; the various deputy Registrars who have worked with us; the stenographers and those who complete the transcripts; the technicians, the interpreters with the difficult job to whom I also extend an apology for the many times we made your work more difficult; and of course, to our ushers and the security officers who have helped us indeed. I also wish to thank all the witnesses that came over to give evidence in this case, helping us in our search for the truth. Witnesses that came from afar, witnesses for the Prosecution, and for the Defence. I also thank the Victims and Witnesses Unit for its assistance, both to the witnesses and to Chambers. Last, but not least, I wish to thank our staff who have worked and worked, including weekends, to help us keep abreast with these proceedings. As I said already, please God, we shall all meet again towards the end of August. I mean, August of this year, of course, when we shall pronounce our final judgement in this case. I said all, but it will not be all. And if this is a misstatement, it's not a misstatement to mislead you, Mr. Ackerman, or you, Ms. Korner. It's because as you know, Ms. Korner will be leaving this Tribunal after the end of this month. And so, please, allow me to say a few words to you, Ms. Korner. Ms. Korner, like me, like Judge Janu and Judge Taya, and like your colleague, Mr. Ackerman, but both of you before us were ahead of us. You were trusted with one of the most difficult cases this Tribunal has had to deal with. You have completed your task admirably, Ms. Korner. You have lived to the traditions of advocacy that you have been so well-trained in. You have been loyal to this Trial Chamber. You have been honest. But above all, you have acted professionally throughout and with the utmost propriety towards the staff, the witnesses, counsel for the Defence, and also the Trial Chamber. Ms. Korner, you have done honour to the legal profession of your country and to the Office of this Tribunal's Prosecutor. For all this I congratulate you, and I thank you. The journey lies ahead for you, too. This time, outside this Tribunal, in your own country, back to the English bar, where you have excelled so well in the past. So as you move to pastures new, but also old, I will not tell you not to look behind because you have a new journey on which you are embarking. Do look behind to your work in this Tribunal, particularly in this case, because your performance here has been inspiring, especially to other officers doing prosecutorial work in this Tribunal. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, Ms. Korner, I wish you all the best on this new journey and venture on which you are about to embark. And please, do look behind while you proceed forward in your career. When we meet again towards the end of August, we will also miss the presence amongst us of Dr. Inga Onsea my ALO who as from June 1st will be joining the Office of the Prosecutor of the Rwanda Tribunal. She, too, is embarking on a new journey. And on behalf of Chambers, I wish to thank her publicly for her excellent work and dedication throughout these two and a half years she worked for us. To her to the adage "don't look behind when the journey lies ahead" does not apply. You should look behind to your work here, to the experience gained here as you move to your new journey to Arusha. I bid you farewell and thank you. The Rwanda Tribunal's gain will be our loss. Missing at the end of August when we pronounce judgement will also be all the interns that have helped us throughout these two and a half years. Many of them are already gone. I wish to them, too, the very best in their -- and every success in their respective careers. We leave this with this while we embark on our long and difficult journey, and we promise you that we will go through the entire journey to the best of our abilities, confident that at the end we will each embark on another journey very happy to look back to this one with pride and satisfaction. What we do with what lies behind us will determine our journey. We leave you with this, and we thank you all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether Anneka has rights of audience and, if not, can I say perhaps on behalf of both of us how very grateful we are for Your Honour's very, very kind words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. You always want to have the last word, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I just want to join in all of your remarks, your thanks to all of the people who have been involved in this. And farewell to Dr. Inga Onsea, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We stand adjourned to a date which will be communicated to you later.
